flawed_step: The first clause, claiming that every finite unit-distance graph is 3-colorable, is false.
counterexample: Let r=√3, s=√11, and q=√33. Take seven points u=(0,0), v=(r,0), a=(r/2,1/2), b=(r/2,-1/2), w=(5r/6,q/6), c=((5r-s)/12,(q+5)/12), and d=((5r+s)/12,(q-5)/12). The pairs at distance exactly 1 are ua, ub, ab, va, vb, uc, ud, cd, wc, wd, and vw. All other squared distances are uv²=uw²=3; ac²=bd²=1/3; ad²=(7-q)/6; bc²=(7+q)/6; vc²=wb²=(9+q)/6; and vd²=wa²=(9-q)/6, none equal to 1. Thus this is an induced unit-distance graph. In any proper 3-coloring, the adjacent vertices a,b use two colors, forcing both u and v to use the third color. Similarly, c,d force u and w to have the same color. Hence v and w have the same color, contradicting the edge vw. Therefore this unit-distance graph is not 3-colorable.
assessment_summary: The explicit seven-point Moser-spindle configuration satisfies the stated unit-distance convention and has no proper 3-coloring, refuting the universal first clause.
